clue.text: This writer with a cosy home being least generous

parts.note: the setter pointing at himself inside his own clue
the article taken at face value
a snug home built by a bird

explanation.surface: A writer sitting in a comfortable house, apparently being tight-fisted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This writer' is the setter's standard way of putting himself in his own clue, and it always gives ME or I. The cosy home belongs to a bird, not to him.
explanation.definitionFit: Mean is the everyday word for tight-fisted, so the superlative is exactly 'least generous'.

clue.text: Apt to pontificate, similar to mad Conservative

indicators.note: Something mad has lost its senses, and with them the sensible order of the letters beside it.

parts.note: nine letters of fodder
c = Conservative, the party abbreviation, joined to the fodder

explanation.surface: A preachy sort being likened to a deranged Tory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Similar to' looks like the comparison the sentence is making and is nine letters of raw material. The Conservative is a single letter, not a person on the bench.
explanation.definitionFit: A moralistic person judges everything by right and wrong and says so at length, which is what pontificating is.

clue.text: Ace leading small part of firm is skilful

indicators.note: What leads goes in front, so the letter it marks is placed at the head of everything else.
'Small' asks for the shortened form of the word beside it rather than the word written out in full.

parts.note: a = ace, as on a playing card
a firm's department is a part of it, and dept is the written short form

explanation.surface: A top card heading a minor division of a company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ace' is a letter here, not a card in the hand. 'Small' is the setter asking for dept rather than department spelt out, a trick worth recognising on sight.
explanation.definitionFit: An adept hand is thoroughly practised at something, so 'skilful' is a plain adjective-for-adjective swap.

clue.text: Up there's a weird river

indicators.note: Weird is out of the natural order, and letters out of their natural order are letters to rearrange.

parts.note: nine letters of fodder, the apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: Someone pointing out an odd-looking river further upstream.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole first half of the clue is the raw material, apostrophe and all, which is why it reads as a finished sentence. The Euphrates is one of the two great rivers of Iraq.
explanation.definitionFit: The Euphrates is a named river of Mesopotamia, so the definition names the class and leaves the solver to supply the example.

clue.text: Cool attempt to keep goal

indicators.note: To keep something is to hold on to it, and a word holding another has it shut inside.

parts.note: an attempt = a try
the goal you are working towards = the end

explanation.surface: An unflustered go at keeping goal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keep goal' is one phrase in the surface and two separate instructions underneath: 'to keep' does the enclosing, 'goal' is the thing enclosed. TRY is the crossword's usual attempt.
explanation.definitionFit: Cool in the fashionable sense — of the moment, what everyone wants — is what trendy means, rather than cool in temperature.

clue.text: Fish starter for dinner very good

indicators.note: A starter is what comes first at table, and what comes first in a word is its opening letter.

parts.note: the opening letter of DINNER
ace = excellent

explanation.surface: The opening course of a meal is excellent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fish starter' reads as one item on a menu, and the clue breaks straight between the two words. A dace is a small silvery fish of slow British rivers.
explanation.definitionFit: A dace is a small freshwater fish of British rivers, so the definition names its kind.

clue.text: Mother the reverse of deranged

indicators.note: The reverse of a word is that word read backwards, which is how the letters here are to be taken.

parts.note: deranged = mad

explanation.surface: A mother is the opposite of unhinged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The reverse of' reads as 'the opposite of' in the surface and means backwards in the wordplay. A dam is an animal's mother, the breeder's word that pairs with sire.
explanation.definitionFit: A dam is the female parent of a horse or other animal, the counterpart of the sire, so 'Mother' is its plain sense in the breeder's vocabulary.

clue.text: Foreign city gone crazy under army officer

indicators.note: in a down clue the second part sits beneath the first

parts.note: COL is the abbreviation for colonel

indicators.note: crazy suggests the letters of gone are jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: An army colonel's posting abroad has driven him round the bend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'under' works because this is a down clue: the reworked letters of 'gone' (OGNE) are written below COL.
explanation.definitionFit: Cologne (Köln) is a major German city on the Rhine, so foreign to a British solver.

clue.text: Some scary entertainment in Sussex town

indicators.note: 'Some' asks for a part of what follows rather than all of it, and the part wanted is a run of consecutive letters.

parts.note: three consecutive letters straddling the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: A bit of frightening fun somewhere in Sussex.
explanation.walkthrough: The hiding place spans the join between two words, which is where these are hardest to spot. Rye is a small hilltop town on the East Sussex coast, a port until the sea withdrew.
explanation.definitionFit: Rye is a town in East Sussex, and the definition pins down which Rye is wanted, since the word is far better known as a grain.

clue.text: Quiet walk around England's capital — introduction for readers

indicators.note: the walk letters go around the capital letter

parts.note: P (piano) is the musical marking for quiet
a ramble is a leisurely walk

indicators.note: a capital here is the first letter of a word

parts.note: its first letter is used

explanation.surface: Instructions to the reader: walk quietly around England's capital city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital' means the initial letter, E, not London; it sits inside RAMBLE after the P.
explanation.definitionFit: A preamble is an opening statement that introduces a document or book to whoever reads it.

clue.text: In favour of experimentation or expressing opposition?

parts.note: pro = in favour of
testing = experimentation

explanation.surface: Somebody who backs experiments — or is dead against them?
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves of the wordplay lean towards approval, PRO and a willingness to try things out, while the whole word means the opposite. The question mark admits the contradiction.
explanation.definitionFit: To protest is to voice objection out loud, so a person protesting is expressing opposition — the very thing the PRO in front appears to rule out.

clue.text: Subsequently had to intervene between left and right

indicators.note: To intervene between two parties is to come in the middle of them, so the piece it marks sits between the other two.

parts.note: l = left
had a meal = ate
r = right

explanation.surface: A peacemaker stepping in between the political left and the political right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Had' is had dinner, not possessed. The left and right of the surface are politics; in the wordplay they are the two single letters that everything else has to fit between.
explanation.definitionFit: Later means at a subsequent time, so the definition is an adverb swapped for an adverb.

clue.text: Fix bet for distinguished old woman?

parts.note: to fix something up is to do it — 'I'll fix that' and 'I'll do that' are the same offer
a wager is a bet

explanation.surface: Rigging a bet on behalf of a grand old lady.
explanation.walkthrough: A dowager is a widow who keeps the title and property of her late husband, so 'distinguished' is carrying the rank. The question mark covers the fact that youth is not actually forbidden.
explanation.definitionFit: A dowager holds her dead husband's title and estate — titled, widowed and grand, which is the picture 'distinguished old woman' sketches.

clue.text: Good-for-nothing shrew — lots needing to be changed!

indicators.note: Something needing to be changed cannot stay as it is, and what changes here is the order of the letters.

parts.note: nine letters of fodder

explanation.surface: A scolding wife with a long list of things she wants altered.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash makes 'lots' look like a fresh thought, when it is the second half of one nine-letter block. 'Good-for-nothing' sits at the front sounding like part of the same complaint.
explanation.definitionFit: Something worthless has no value at all, and 'good-for-nothing' is the everyday idiom for exactly that emptiness.

clue.text: Something protective shut up to keep warmth in

indicators.note: To keep something is to hold on to it, and a word holding another has it shut inside.
'In' says where the warmth goes — within the letters around it rather than alongside them.

parts.note: sh! is the hiss that tells somebody to shut up
warmth = heat

explanation.surface: A protective covering closed up so that no warmth can escape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shut up' is the hiss, SH, and not the closing of anything. A sheath is the close-fitting case a blade or a cable lives in, which is why 'protective' needs no qualifier.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheath is a close-fitting cover for a knife or a cable, there to guard whatever sits inside it.

clue.text: Former lover not attractive? Elucidate

parts.note: an ex is a former partner
plain = not good-looking

explanation.surface: An old flame who was never much to look at.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark softens the rudeness of calling an ex plain. 'Plain' in the looks sense is the one step to take, since the word more often means simple or unadorned.
explanation.definitionFit: To explain is to make a thing clear, and elucidate is the formal verb for the same act.

clue.text: Silver revolver finally carried by spy

indicators.note: the letter is held within the word for spy

parts.note: a secret agent is a spy

indicators.note: only the closing letter of revolver is taken

parts.note: its last letter is used

explanation.surface: A spy carries a silver revolver, like something from a thriller.
explanation.walkthrough: Argent is the heraldic word for silver, from Latin argentum.
explanation.definitionFit: Argent is the heraldic tincture of silver, and a poetic word for the metal itself.

clue.text: Place of rest left in the morning commotion

parts.note: the place you rest in
l = left
a.m. = ante meridiem, before noon

explanation.surface: A restful place abandoned in the morning, and the uproar that follows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' is the letter L, not the verb the surface wants. Bedlam was the Hospital of St Mary of Bethlehem in London, the old asylum whose nickname became the word for uproar.
explanation.definitionFit: Bedlam is noisy confusion, the sense the London madhouse of that name left behind in the language.

clue.text: Naughty kid leading idiots endlessly blocking state

indicators.note: What leads goes in front, so the naughty kid heads everything that follows.

parts.note: an imp is a mischievous child
ASSES with its final letter removed

explanation.surface: A mischievous child at the head of a crowd of fools who are in the way.
explanation.walkthrough: IMP is the crossword's standard naughty child. 'Idiots' has to be the plural ASSES, since docking the singular would leave the word a letter short.
explanation.definitionFit: An impasse is a deadlock — a position in which nothing can move because every way out is blocked.

clue.text: The fellow's penning notice: "This is a deadly place"

indicators.note: To pen something is to shut it in a pen, so the word doing the penning closes round the word after it.

parts.note: the fellow's = he's, with the apostrophe dropped
an ad is a notice placed in a paper

explanation.surface: A man writing out a warning that somewhere is lethal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penning' reads as writing and means enclosing. Hades is the Greek underworld, the realm of the dead rather than anywhere that would kill a visitor, which is what the quotation marks smooth over.
explanation.definitionFit: Hades is the Greek realm of the dead, so the definition names it by its inhabitants rather than by any danger it poses.

clue.text: Gosh, bounder set up country house!

indicators.note: In a down clue 'set up' means stood on end, so the letters are read from the bottom upwards.

parts.note: ah! is the cry of surprise
a cad is a bounder, the old British word for a man who behaves dishonourably

explanation.surface: Astonishment that a scoundrel has set himself up with a place in the country.
explanation.walkthrough: A dacha is the Russian country cottage, the weekend retreat outside the city. 'Set up' can only mean reverse because the entry runs downwards, and the exclamation mark keeps the surface innocent.
explanation.definitionFit: A dacha is the Russian second home in the country, a cottage or villa used at weekends and through the summer.

clue.text: The old man not moving, with minimal energy — sugary lozenge needed?

indicators.note: Minimal asks for the very least there is of the word beside it, and the least of a word is one letter.

parts.note: the old man = Dad, the family nickname
still = motionless
e is the scientific symbol for energy

explanation.surface: An elderly father sitting motionless and listless, who might fancy a sweet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The old man' is the family nickname for Dad, which is why it gives two letters rather than describing anybody elderly. A pastille is the small chewy sweet sold in a paper tube.
explanation.definitionFit: A pastille is a small sweetened lozenge, sucked for pleasure or for a sore throat, so the definition is a plain description of the thing.

clue.text: Money invested in important industry

indicators.note: To be invested in something is to be placed inside it, so the letters wanted sit inside the words that follow.

parts.note: three consecutive letters running straight across the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: Cash put into a major industry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Invested in' is the rare indicator that suits its surface perfectly, since money really does go into an industry. Tin is dated slang for money and survives mainly in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: Tin is old British slang for cash, the same sort of joke as brass or dough.

clue.text: Charlie greeting Greek character

parts.note: c = Charlie in the radio alphabet
hi is the everyday greeting

explanation.surface: A man named Charlie saying hello.
explanation.walkthrough: Charlie is C in the NATO radio alphabet, the list that also gives alpha, bravo and delta. Chi is the Greek letter written X, the one that stands in for Christ in Xmas.
explanation.definitionFit: Chi is a letter of the Greek alphabet, so 'character' is used in its typographic sense rather than for a person.

clue.text: Cathedral dignitary losing head before long

indicators.note: the first letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: a canon is a member of the clergy attached to a cathedral

explanation.surface: A senior cathedral cleric will soon be decapitated.
explanation.walkthrough: Anon is the old-fashioned word for soon, as in 'more anon'.
explanation.definitionFit: Anon is an archaic adverb meaning soon or shortly, as in 'I'll see you anon'.

clue.text: Wild man tugs wild horse

indicators.note: Wild means untamed and unruly, and unruly letters will not stay in the order they are given.

parts.note: seven letters of fodder

explanation.surface: A rough-looking man hauling at an untamed horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wild' appears twice and does a different job each time: the first shuffles, the second defines. Mustangs are the feral descendants of horses the Spanish brought to America.
explanation.definitionFit: A mustang is the feral horse of the American plains, running loose rather than bred, which is what the definition describes.
